claims.text: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi is a high-entropy alloy system.
Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi can be produced by arc melting followed by drop casting into a water-cooled copper mold.
Undoped Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi normally crystallizes under the stated cooling conditions.
An oxygen-modified alloy with composition (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 can be prepared by arc melting and drop casting.
The undoped and oxygen-doped alloys can be processed under comparable arc-melting and drop-casting conditions.
Interstitial oxygen forms localized oxygen complexes or ordered oxygen clusters in this alloy.
Localized oxygen complexes increase lattice distortion and local atomic disorder.
Interstitial oxygen disrupts regular atomic arrangements and increases local packing frustration.
The oxygen-induced structural disruption hinders nucleation of crystalline phases.
Kinetic hindrance of crystallization caused by oxygen promotes glass formation.
Small interstitial oxygen additions enhance the glass-forming ability of Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi.
Oxygen doping will produce a greater amorphous fraction than the undoped alloy under the same processing conditions.
Oxygen doping will increase the glass-transition temperature.
Enhanced glass-forming ability will be evidenced by a higher critical cooling rate for crystallization.
The beneficial effect of oxygen is limited to a finite concentration range.
Excess oxygen can promote oxide formation and reduce amorphous stability.
Interstitial oxygen is known to affect lattice ordering, damping, and dislocation mobility in related high-entropy alloys.
Direct evidence linking oxygen addition to enhanced glass-forming ability in this system has not been established.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts enhanced glass-forming ability, but lists a higher critical cooling rate as supporting evidence. Glass-forming ability is conventionally enhanced when the minimum cooling rate needed to avoid crystallization decreases, so the stated direction is internally inconsistent unless 'critical cooling rate for crystallization' is defined differently.

The mechanism invokes kinetic hindrance of crystallization but then describes glass formation as arising from a lower thermodynamic driving-force requirement for forming an ordered lattice. This mixes kinetic and thermodynamic explanations and does not coherently connect them.
